opening_message:
Ticket 1: Dominic Taylor (employee ID E004) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E004.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Dominic Taylor (E004) is a full-time Engineer. Requested write access to Source Code is within policy (write allowed for full-time employees; Engineer owns Source Code). Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E004 (Dominic Taylor) as a contractor with basic security training, which differs from the earlier note's full_time entry. Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Basic training limits to read; requested write exceeds policy, so recommend read.
reason: There is a conflict between the HR note (full-time Engineer, recommending write) and the Security note (contractor with basic security training, recommending read). Both agents report looking up employment type in their own databases. Under the contractor interpretation, the maximum allowed for Source Code is read (write requires advanced training, and Dominic has only basic training), so the requested write exceeds policy and must be capped at read. Given the material dispute over employment status, I apply the more restrictive, least-privilege interpretation to avoid granting write access that may exceed policy.
